d.1:3:
Sets a function that builds a tooltip view shown while the pointer rests over this element.

The tooltip is hidden as soon as the pointer leaves the element, so the user cannot move onto it. Use
[`Interactivity::hoverable_tooltip`] for a tooltip that stays open. A long press on a touch screen also shows
it. This is the imperative equivalent of [`StatefulInteractiveElement::tooltip`].

# Panics

Panics in debug builds if a tooltip is already set on this element.

Creates a binding from the parts that a keymap file provides.

`keystrokes` is split on spaces and each part is parsed with [`Keystroke::parse`]. Each
keystroke is then passed to `keyboard_mapper`, and `use_key_equivalents` asks it for the
layout-dependent mapping. On macOS, that replaces a key with the character the current
layout types for it. For bindings from a keymap file, `action_input` is the JSON the action
was built from. Pass `None` when there is none.

# Errors

Returns [`InvalidKeystrokeError`] if any keystroke fails to parse. The context is already
parsed, so this function doesn't check it.

d.1:3:
Creates a binding that runs `action` when `keystrokes` is typed in `context`.

`keystrokes` is a whitespace-separated sequence of
[keystrokes](Keystroke::parse), such as `"cmd-s"` or `"ctrl-k ctrl-s"`.
`context` is a [key context predicate](KeyBindingContextPredicate::parse),
such as `"Editor"` or `"Editor && mode == insert"`. Pass `None` to make the binding apply
everywhere, which counts as the deepest context for precedence.

Bindings made here use the keys as written. They never go through the platform's keyboard
mapping, so use this for bindings in code.

# Panics

Panics if any keystroke or the context fails to parse. Use [`KeyBinding::load`] to get an
error instead.

# Examples

```standalone_crate
use gpui::{KeyBinding, actions};

actions!(binding_new_docs, [Save]);

let binding = KeyBinding::new("secondary-s", Save, Some("Editor"));
assert_eq!(binding.keystrokes().len(), 1);
```

Parse a string in the same format as the keymap's context field.

A basic equivalence check against a set of identifiers can performed by
simply writing a string:

`StatusBar` -> A predicate that will match a context with the identifier `StatusBar`

You can also specify a key-value pair:

`mode == visible` -> A predicate that will match a context with the key `mode`
                     with the value `visible`

And a logical operations combining these two checks:

`StatusBar && mode == visible` -> A predicate that will match a context with the
                                  identifier `StatusBar` and the key `mode`
                                  with the value `visible`


There is also a special child `>` operator that will match a predicate that is
below another predicate:

`StatusBar > mode == visible` -> A predicate that will match a context identifier `StatusBar`
                                 and a child context that has the key `mode` with the
                                 value `visible`

This syntax supports `!=`, `||` and `&&` as logical operators.
You can also preface an operation or check with a `!` to negate it.

d.1:3:
Parses a predicate such as `Editor && !ReadOnly` or `Panel > Editor`.

The grammar, from the tightest-binding rule to the loosest, is:

- **Atoms.** An identifier, such as `Editor`, matches a context with that name. An identifier
  is letters, digits, `_` and `-`. The characters `>`, `<`, `~`, `"` and `?` can also
  appear after the first character, so write `Panel > Editor` with spaces. The text
  `Panel>Editor` is one identifier.
- **Parentheses.** `( ... )` groups a predicate.
- **Negation.** `!` applies to the atom or parenthesized group after it, so `!a && b` is
  `(!a) && b`. Use `!(a && b)` to negate a group.
- **Equality.** `key == value` and `key != value` compare the value of an entry. Both sides
  must be plain identifiers, so `mode == "full"` is an error.
- **`&&`** binds tighter than **`||`**. So `a || b && c` is `a || (b && c)`.
- **Descendant.** `parent > child` binds loosest, so `a && b > c` is `(a && b) > c`. It is
  left-associative: `A > B > C` is `(A > B) > C`.

The keymap guide has the same rules as a table.

# Errors

Returns an error for an unbalanced parenthesis, a missing operand, an operator the grammar
doesn't have, a `==` or `!=` whose operands aren't identifiers, or any leftover text.

# Examples

```
# use gpui::KeyBindingContextPredicate;
let predicate = KeyBindingContextPredicate::parse("Pane > (Editor || Terminal) && !ReadOnly")
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(predicate.to_string(), "Pane > (Editor || Terminal) && !ReadOnly");
assert!(KeyBindingContextPredicate::parse("mode == \"full\"").is_err());
```

See [contexts](crate::_documentation::concepts::contexts) and
[keyboard input](crate::_documentation::guides::keyboard) for when contexts apply.

d.1:3:
Parses a context such as `Editor` or `Editor mode=full`.

The text is a list of entries separated by whitespace. Each entry is either an identifier,
such as `Editor`, or a key-value pair written `key=value` or `key = value`. Identifier
characters are letters, digits, `_` and `-`. An entry whose key is already present is
ignored, so the first one wins. Returns an error for text that isn't a list of such
entries, such as `.` or `=insert`.

This takes entries only. Operators such as `&&` and `>` aren't part of this format. Use
[`KeyBindingContextPredicate::parse`] to write a predicate.

# Examples

```
# use gpui::{KeyContext, SharedString};
let context = KeyContext::parse("Panel Editor mode = insert").unwrap();
assert!(context.contains("Panel"));
assert_eq!(context.primary().unwrap().key, SharedString::from("Panel"));
```

d.1:3:
Iterates over the bindings that run `action`, in the order they were added.

Bindings disabled by a later [`NoAction`](crate::NoAction) or [`Unbind`](crate::Unbind) are
left out. This ignores key contexts, so a binding is included even when it can't fire in the
current focus. To find the bindings that apply now, use
[`Window::bindings_for_action`](crate::Window::bindings_for_action). For a shortcut label,
use the last binding, which was added most recently.

Returns a list of bindings that match the given input, and a boolean indicating whether or
not more bindings might match if the input was longer. Bindings are returned in precedence
order (higher precedence first, reverse of the order they were added to the keymap).

Precedence is defined by the depth in the tree (matches on the Editor take precedence over
matches on the Pane, then the Workspace, etc.). Bindings with no context are treated as the
same as the deepest context.

In the case of multiple bindings at the same depth, the ones added to the keymap later take
precedence. User bindings are added after built-in bindings so that they take precedence.

If a user has disabled a binding with `"x": null` it will not be returned. Disabled bindings
are evaluated with the same precedence rules so you can disable a rule in a given context
only.

d.1:3:
Returns the bindings that match `input` in `context_stack`, and whether a longer input
could still match a binding.

The first value holds the matching bindings, highest precedence first. The second value is
`true` when some binding needs more keystrokes than `input`, so the caller should wait for
the next keystroke.

Precedence works as follows:

- **Depth.** A binding's depth is the deepest point in `context_stack` where its predicate
  matches. A binding in a deeper context wins over one in a shallower context. A binding
  without a context is as deep as the stack, so it is at least as deep as any
  context-specific binding. At equal depth, the order rule below decides.
- **Order.** At the same depth, the binding added later wins.
- **`NoAction`.** A winning [`NoAction`](crate::NoAction) removes the lower-precedence
  bindings for the same keystrokes, unless they come from a stronger source. See
  [`KeyBindingMetaIndex`](crate::KeyBindingMetaIndex).
- **`Unbind`.** A winning [`Unbind`](crate::Unbind) removes the lower-precedence binding for
  the same keystrokes that runs the action it names, whatever that binding's context.

Several bindings can be returned, because a match that isn't suppressed stays in the list.

# Examples

```standalone_crate
use gpui::{Action, KeyBinding, KeyContext, Keymap, Keystroke, actions};

actions!(input_docs, [Save, Format]);

let keymap = Keymap::new(vec![
    KeyBinding::new("cmd-s", Format, Some("Workspace")),
    KeyBinding::new("cmd-s", Save, Some("Editor")),
]);

// The `Editor` binding is at depth 2 and the `Workspace` binding at depth 1.
let (bindings, _) = keymap.bindings_for_input(
    &[Keystroke::parse("cmd-s").unwrap()],
    &[
        KeyContext::parse("Workspace").unwrap(),
        KeyContext::parse("Editor").unwrap(),
    ],
);
assert_eq!(bindings[0].action().name(), "input_docs::Save");
```

not more bindings might match if the input was longer. Bindings are returned in precedence
order (higher precedence first, reverse of the order they were added to the keymap).

Precedence is defined by the depth in the tree (matches on the Editor take precedence over
matches on the Pane, then the Workspace, etc.). Bindings with no context are treated as the
same as the deepest context.

In the case of multiple bindings at the same depth, the ones added to the keymap later take
precedence. User bindings are added after built-in bindings so that they take precedence.

If a user has disabled a binding with `"x": null` it will not be returned. Disabled bindings
are evaluated with the same precedence rules so you can disable a rule in a given context
only.
